title: Patient-Centric Healthcare 5.0
subtitle: AI for Better Conversations, Safer Decisions, Professional Impact and Research

cases.title: EHR-embedded X-ray triage and no-show prediction
cases.setting: Health Center Nis; MEDIS.NET across 25 facilities
cases.ai: VGG19-based chest X-ray classification plus appointment-attendance prediction embedded in the EHR
cases.result: The article reports about 92% X-ray classification accuracy and a substantial reduction in no-shows when models and staff action were combined.
cases.evidence: 2025 operational case study and local model validation
cases.limitation: Single health-system context; model performance and workflow results require external and local validation.
cases.human: Radiologist signs the report; staff decide outreach or scheduling action.
cases.lesson: Embed probability in the workflow; do not hide decision ownership.
cases.question: Which decision should remain visibly human even if the prediction is accurate?

cases.title: What family physicians expect and fear
cases.setting: Qatar Primary Health Care Corporation; 102 eligible family-physician responses
cases.ai: Survey of perceived clinical, administrative and public-health applications
cases.result: 78.4% reported AI awareness; respondents perceived value in task management but raised confidentiality, accountability and patient-satisfaction concerns.
cases.limitation: Self-reported perceptions from 102 of 724 invited physicians; not a clinical-effectiveness study.
cases.human: Physicians asked for training, governance and clear accountability.
cases.lesson: Adoption is a trust and operating-model problem, not only a model problem.
cases.question: What assurance would your colleagues need before using a new AI tool?

cases.title: Generative AI in case-based medical learning
cases.setting: Chengdu Medical College; 79 students, control n=40 and AI group n=39
cases.ai: Kimi Chat 2.0 used to research and present a liver-cancer case
cases.result: Assignment time was 2.6 vs 5.5 hours; final scores 77.3±4.3 vs 66.5±5.4; teacher questions fell from 35 to 10.
cases.limitation: Two intact classes in one course; not randomised across institutions; learning and grading findings should not be treated as clinical outcomes.
cases.human: Faculty discussion remains essential for reasoning, originality and challenge.
cases.lesson: AI raises the floor and compresses search time; it can also homogenise thinking.
cases.question: How do we save time without reducing productive struggle?

cases.title: AI-supported scenario planning for medical curricula
cases.setting: Trinity College Dublin; one workshop with 28 participants
cases.ai: ChatGPT narratives, MidJourney visuals and Murf.AI narration for four 2035 scenarios
cases.result: Participants converged on systems thinking, patient-centredness, continuous learning, participatory health, sustainability and technological adaptability.
cases.limitation: One workshop, no patient representatives, possible groupthink and framing effects; not universally generalisable.
cases.human: Facilitators reviewed and refined all AI outputs; participants chose competencies and actions.
cases.lesson: AI can make futures tangible; people must choose values and priorities.
cases.question: Which capability remains essential in every plausible future?

cases.title: Why clinicians ignore alerts—and how design can restore trust
cases.setting: Six experienced US clinicians discussing the Epic Sepsis Model and a prototype
cases.ai: Trend and uncertainty visualisation, ranked information needs and what-if simulation
cases.result: Clinicians described the redesigned system more as a collaborator than a static score.
cases.evidence: 2024 qualitative study and human-AI prototype evaluation
cases.limitation: Very small qualitative sample and prototype setting; not an outcome or safety trial.
cases.human: Clinician interprets risk, orders information and decides action.
cases.lesson: Timely, explainable and actionable support can beat another interruptive alert.
cases.question: Does this alert arrive before the decision—and tell us what could reduce uncertainty?

cases.title: The real workflow cost and payoff of ambient documentation
cases.setting: Five-practice deployment described in a DBA dissertation, triangulated with multi-site peer-reviewed ambient-scribe evidence
cases.ai: Conversation capture with consent and a draft note for clinician review
cases.result: Reports describe initial resistance, new review work and potential reductions in after-hours EHR time and burden after adoption.
cases.evidence: Implementation dissertation plus growing health-system observational evidence
cases.limitation: Product, setting, adoption maturity and outcome measures vary; product-specific safety and local effect require validation.
cases.human: Clinician or designated reviewer edits and signs; organisation owns consent, retention and audit.
cases.lesson: Time saved at the keyboard creates a new quality-assurance workflow.
cases.question: Who reviews the reviewer—and what error would stop the pilot?

cases.title: Why a visible explanation is necessary—but not sufficient
cases.setting: 2025 reference chapter covering imaging, drug discovery and personalised medicine
cases.ai: Heatmaps, attention maps and feature attribution to expose model influences
cases.result: The chapter illustrates how explanation can support audit, teaching and clinician sense-checking.
cases.evidence: Narrative reference chapter with illustrative case applications
cases.limitation: An explanation can be plausible yet unstable or misleading; explainability is not proof of accuracy or benefit.
cases.human: Professional compares the explanation with intended use, validation and patient context.
cases.lesson: Ask why, for whom and under what validation—not only what the model predicted.
cases.question: Is the explanation clinically meaningful or merely decorative?

universal_wrapper: You are supporting a synthetic healthcare education exercise. You are not the treating clinician and must not replace professional judgement. Do not provide a final diagnosis, prescribe, change a dose, provide reassurance or instruct anyone to delay urgent care. Separate supplied facts, patient-reported information, professional observations, assumptions, unknowns and AI-generated hypotheses. Do not invent findings, medicines, laboratory results, citations or guidelines. Identify red flags and information requiring urgent professional review. Use only the information and approved sources supplied. End with a section titled 'Human decision and verification required'.

prompts.title: Consultation continuity
prompts.purpose: Turn a synthetic conversation into a reviewable draft without inventing clinical facts.
prompts.tool: ChatGPT; compare with Heidi or Nabla
prompts.prompt: Using the synthetic consultation transcript below, create: (1) a source-grounded draft encounter summary, (2) a problem-information list, (3) medication-reconciliation questions, (4) a plain-language patient summary, (5) three teach-back questions, and (6) follow-up and escalation items. Tag every statement [PATIENT REPORTED], [PROFESSIONAL OBSERVATION], [UNKNOWN] or [NEEDS VERIFICATION]. Do not invent examination findings, diagnosis, medication, dose, investigation, reassurance or follow-up decision. Transcript: [PASTE SYNTHETIC TRANSCRIPT]
prompts.expected: Tagged draft note, patient summary, questions and escalation items
prompts.checkpoint: Reconcile facts and medicines; check red flags, consent, local language and record policy before sign-off.
prompts.failure: Invented findings or a polished draft copied into the record without review.
prompts.discussion: What attention did the tool return—and what new verification work did it create?

prompts.title: Diagnostic reasoning without outsourcing diagnosis
prompts.purpose: Expose hypotheses, missing information and urgency.
prompts.tool: ChatGPT; compare with DxGPT and a clinical evidence tool
prompts.prompt: Using only the synthetic case below: (1) write a one-sentence problem representation without declaring a diagnosis; (2) group hypotheses as common/likely, dangerous must-not-miss, and alternative explanations; (3) for each, list supporting information, contradictory information, missing information, red flags, time sensitivity and evidence that must be verified; (4) identify the five questions or observations most likely to change urgency; and (5) state what a licensed clinician must decide. Do not recommend treatment or invent probabilities. Case: [PASTE SYNTHETIC CASE]
prompts.checkpoint: Check urgent red flags, primary evidence, local protocol and patient context; clinician owns diagnosis and disposition.
prompts.failure: A plausible list mistaken for a diagnosis or a reason to delay escalation.
prompts.discussion: Did the output widen attention or create noise?

prompts.title: Medication-reconciliation discussion
prompts.purpose: Surface possible medicine issues that require verification.
prompts.tool: ChatGPT; compare with Epocrates, Lexicomp, Micromedex or an approved reference
prompts.input: Synthetic medicine list plus allergies and relevant context
prompts.prompt: Review the synthetic medication information below. Do not recommend starting, stopping or changing any medicine. Create a verification checklist covering possible duplication, interaction, allergy conflict, renal/hepatic considerations, pregnancy/lactation if relevant, indication uncertainty, adherence, OTC/supplement/traditional-medicine use, monitoring and missing name/strength/formulation/route/frequency. Separate confirmed facts, potential issues to verify and missing information. List questions for the patient and prescriber/pharmacist, plus the approved drug-information sources that must be checked. Information: [PASTE SYNTHETIC LIST]
prompts.checkpoint: Licensed prescriber/pharmacist checks labels, formulary, renal/hepatic context and local protocol.
prompts.failure: Model invents an interaction or silently changes a dose.
prompts.discussion: Which issue is a signal—and which is a verified fact?

prompts.title: Patient-education asset
prompts.purpose: Convert approved evidence into actionable plain language.
prompts.tool: ChatGPT plus Canva/Gamma; bilingual review may use Bhashini
prompts.input: Approved source excerpt and audience definition
prompts.prompt: Using only the approved source excerpt below, draft a one-page patient handout for [AUDIENCE] at class 6–8 reading level. Include a short title, five practical actions, medicine-taking reminders without products or doses, monitoring, routine follow-up, three urgent red flags, three teach-back questions, source, review date, reviewer placeholder and AI-assistance disclosure. Mark unsupported statements [REVIEW]. Provide a draft Hindi version, marking medical terms for bilingual professional review. Do not invent statistics, guarantees or clinical advice outside the source. Source: [PASTE APPROVED SOURCE]
prompts.expected: Plain-language handout with red flags and teach-back
prompts.checkpoint: Clinical meaning, translation, accessibility, source, version and reviewer approval.
prompts.failure: Unsafe simplification, mistranslation or an unsupported promise.
prompts.discussion: Can the patient act safely—and is routine advice separated from urgent action?

prompts.title: Redesigning an unhelpful clinical alert
prompts.purpose: Apply the SepsisLab design lesson to a synthetic alert.
prompts.prompt: Evaluate the synthetic alert below without making a patient-specific treatment recommendation. Analyse timeliness, false-positive burden, false-negative risk, explanation, uncertainty, actionability, workflow interruption, override, escalation and audit trail. Redesign it to show what changed, why it appeared, current uncertainty, information that could reduce uncertainty, required professional review, override/documentation path, pilot metrics and stop criteria. Alert: [PASTE SYNTHETIC ALERT]
prompts.expected: Before/after alert specification and pilot measures
prompts.checkpoint: Clinical governance approves intended use, escalation, thresholds and monitoring.
prompts.failure: A more attractive alert that still arrives late or triggers unowned action.
prompts.discussion: Does the redesign help before the decision—or simply explain after it?

prompts.title: Ambient-scribe pilot plan
prompts.purpose: Design a controlled implementation with quality assurance.
prompts.tool: ChatGPT; compare with Heidi/Nabla governance settings
prompts.prompt: Design a six-week controlled ambient-scribe pilot. Include intended and excluded uses; patient notice/consent; minimum necessary data; clinician and scribe-reviewer responsibilities; note sampling; error taxonomy; hallucination and omission monitoring; patient-experience, clinician-time and after-hours documentation measures; safety escalation; rollback; stop criteria; and final continue/redesign/stop decision. Do not assume time saving proves safety.
prompts.expected: Six-week pilot charter and measurement plan
prompts.checkpoint: Privacy, clinical governance, IT/security and accountable service owner approve the pilot.
prompts.failure: Plug-and-play rollout without consent, sampling or stop rules.
prompts.discussion: Who reviews the reviewer—and what error stops the pilot?

prompts.title: Pharma medical-information and safety triage
prompts.purpose: Separate scientific response, off-label handling and immediate safety escalation.
prompts.tool: ChatGPT discussion prompt; compare with approved medical-information/PV workflow
prompts.prompt: Analyse the synthetic medical-information interaction. Create: the exact unsolicited scientific question; minimum information needed; approved sources; a neutral response outline; statements requiring medical/legal/regulatory review; possible off-label elements requiring medical-information handling; possible adverse-event or product-quality information requiring immediate escalation; follow-up commitments; and documentation requirements. Do not create promotional claims, assess causality, minimise an event or delay escalation. Interaction: [PASTE SYNTHETIC INTERACTION]
prompts.expected: Neutral inquiry plan plus explicit safety/PQC escalation flags
prompts.checkpoint: Medical information, pharmacovigilance and MLR follow the approved SOP; safety escalation is immediate.
prompts.failure: A polished response that misses or delays an adverse-event report.
prompts.discussion: Which part belongs to medical information, PV, product quality or MLR?

prompts.title: Explainable-AI vendor evaluation
prompts.purpose: Turn marketing claims into an auditable due-diligence conversation.
prompts.input: Vendor product description and evidence summary
prompts.prompt: Evaluate the medical-AI product description. Build a due-diligence table for intended use/user, target population, setting, validation population and comparator, sensitivity/specificity, false positives/negatives, subgroup performance, external validation, explainability method and clinical meaning, workflow integration, override, audit trail, data location/retention, jurisdiction-specific regulatory status, evidence gaps, India applicability, vendor questions, reasons to pilot and reasons not to pilot. Do not infer approval or effectiveness from marketing language. Description: [PASTE]
prompts.checkpoint: Clinical, regulatory, privacy, security and procurement reviewers verify original evidence and status.
prompts.failure: Decorative heatmaps treated as proof of correctness.
prompts.discussion: Is the explanation clinically meaningful or merely persuasive?

prompts.title: Socratic medical teaching
prompts.purpose: Use AI to strengthen reasoning rather than reveal an answer immediately.
prompts.input: Synthetic teaching case and learner level
prompts.prompt: Act as a Socratic facilitator for the synthetic case. Do not reveal the answer immediately. Ask the learner to create a problem representation; propose common, dangerous and alternative hypotheses; identify evidence for/against; identify missing information and urgency; challenge one assumption; introduce one verified source; ask the learner to revise; then provide feedback with a transparent rubric and identify unsupported AI-generated information. Case: [PASTE]
prompts.expected: Staged questions, revised reasoning and rubric feedback
prompts.checkpoint: Faculty verifies content and preserves learner effort, dialogue and originality.
prompts.failure: Instant answers reduce productive struggle and create look-alike submissions.
prompts.discussion: Did the AI promote reasoning or replace it?

prompts.title: Professional projection
prompts.purpose: Draft a credible evidence-based professional post with visible boundaries.
prompts.input: Approved evidence, audience and professional role
prompts.prompt: Using only the approved evidence below, draft a 150–200 word professional post for [DOCTOR / MEDICAL-AFFAIRS PROFESSIONAL] to [EDUCATE PATIENTS / EDUCATE PEERS / DISCUSS AN EVIDENCE GAP]. Include one evidence-based message, one practical implication, one limitation, a visible source, AI-assistance disclosure and an invitation to professional discussion—not individual treatment advice. Do not add product promotion, off-label claims, exaggerated certainty or authority beyond the stated role. Evidence: [PASTE]
prompts.expected: Concise, sourced and bounded professional post
prompts.checkpoint: Clinical/MLR review, citation, disclosure, version owner and publication approval.
prompts.failure: Authority signalling, promotion or advice without patient context.
prompts.discussion: Does the post prove usefulness before claiming authority?

prompts.title: Rapid evidence map
prompts.purpose: Create a reproducible starting map without fabricating citations.
prompts.prompt: Convert the question into a transparent rapid-research workflow. Produce PICO; concepts and synonyms; a draft PubMed Boolean query; inclusion and exclusion criteria; evidence-extraction fields; citation-verification checklist; bias/applicability questions; uncertainty log; and a statement of what this rapid review cannot conclude. Do not invent citations. Label every citation [UNVERIFIED] until located in PubMed, a registry or the original publication. Question: [PASTE]
prompts.expected: Search strategy, extraction frame and uncertainty log
prompts.checkpoint: Every citation and extracted field is verified in the original source; methods and limitations are documented.
prompts.failure: A fluent synthesis with fabricated or mischaracterised studies.
prompts.discussion: Which evidence was actually verified—and why is this not a systematic review?
